title: Git and GitHub workflow
summary: Commits as save points, branches as safe sandboxes, pull requests as the door to production, and how to undo a bad change without panic.
youWillLearn: Why a commit is a save point you can always return to
How branches keep unfinished work away from the live app
What a pull request adds: a preview, checks and a second pair of eyes
How to undo a bad deploy with git revert, and why a leaked secret needs more than that

glossary.repository: The project folder plus its full history of changes. Your laptop has a copy, GitHub has a copy.
glossary.commit: A saved snapshot of your files with a short message and a unique id, like a named save point in a game.
glossary.branch: A separate line of commits where you can work without touching the main line.
glossary.main: The branch that holds the real, approved version of the app. On Vercel, pushing to it deploys production.
glossary.push: Upload your new commits from your laptop to GitHub.
glossary.pull request: A page on GitHub that asks to merge one branch into another, with the diff, comments, checks and a preview link.
glossary.diff: The exact lines added and removed by a change, shown in red and green.
glossary.merge: Bring the commits of one branch into another, so both lines of work become one.
glossary.revert: A new commit that does the exact opposite of an old one. It undoes the change without erasing history.
glossary.force push: Overwriting the history on GitHub with your local version. It can silently delete other people's commits.

steps.title: It worked yesterday
body: Maya asks Claude Code to add tags to Notely. It edits fourteen files and pushes straight to production. Now the AI summary button throws an error.
Which of the fourteen changes broke it? What did the files look like yesterday? Without a history, Maya can only guess and patch on top of the damage.

callout.text: Editing a Figma file with version history turned off. One bad hour of changes, and there is no "restore this version" button.

scene.caption: Changes go from the laptop straight to the live app. Nothing records what changed.

steps.title: Commits: save points with names
body: Git fixes this with commits. Each commit is a snapshot of the whole project, with a short message and a unique id like 7c2e.
The commits line up into a history. Any snapshot can be opened, compared with another, or restored. The full history lives in the repository, on the laptop and on GitHub.

scene.caption: A history of named snapshots. If the newest one is broken, the one before it still exists.

steps.title: Branches: work beside the live app
body: A branch is a separate line of commits. Main holds what is live. New work goes on its own branch, like feature/tags.
Maya can commit half-finished tags all afternoon. Production keeps running the last good commit on main, untouched, until she decides the work is ready.

callout.text: Duplicating a page in Figma to explore a new layout. The original stays clean for the client, and you merge the good ideas back later.

scene.caption: Tags live on their own branch. Production still runs main.

steps.title: Small commits, clear messages
body: A good commit does one thing: "Add tags column", then "Show tag chips", then "Filter by tag". When something breaks, small commits point at the cause.
Before each commit, read the diff. It shows every line added and removed. Then push the branch to GitHub so the work is backed up.

callout.text: When two branches change the same lines, Git stops and asks which version wins. That is a merge conflict. Short-lived branches keep conflicts rare and small. If Claude Code resolves one, read the result: it can quietly drop the other side's change.

code.code:
git switch -c feature/tags      # new branch
git status                      # what changed?
git diff                        # read every line
git add src/components/TagChip.tsx
git commit -m "Show tag chips on notes"
git push -u origin feature/tags
code.caption: -u links the local branch to the one on GitHub, so later a plain git push is enough.

scene.caption: Each small commit on the branch is pushed to GitHub as a backup.

steps.title: Pull requests: the door to main
body: When the branch is ready, Maya opens a pull request on GitHub. It shows the full diff and invites comments.
Two useful things happen on their own. Vercel builds a preview URL of this exact branch. Automatic checks run, like tests and type checks. Nothing reaches production until someone presses Merge.

callout.text: Working alone? Still use pull requests. The preview link is free QA, and the PR page is a written record a client can read.

scene.caption: The pull request gathers a preview, checks and a review before anything goes live.

steps.title: Letting Claude Code drive Git
body: Claude Code can run the whole loop: create the branch, commit in small steps, push, and open the PR with the gh command line tool.
Your job moves from typing commands to reviewing. Read the PR diff like a design crit: does every changed file belong to this feature? Then click through the preview, and only then merge.

code.code:
gh pr create --title "Add tags to notes" \
  --body "Adds tags column, chips and filter"
gh pr checks --watch  # wait for green
gh pr merge --squash  # one tidy commit on main
code.caption: --squash folds the branch's commits into one commit on main, which is simple to revert later.

callout.text: Ask it to work on a branch, never on main. Check the diff for files you did not expect: lockfiles, config, migrations, .env. Are commit messages specific? Did it push with --force? If so, ask why.

scene.caption: Checks are green, the preview looks right, so the PR is merged and main deploys.

steps.title: Undo with revert, not by hand
body: A bug slipped through and production breaks. Do not start editing files in a hurry. Use revert.

git revert creates a new commit that does the exact opposite of the bad one. History stays intact, main deploys again, and the app is back where it was. On GitHub, a merged PR even has a Revert button.

code.code:
git switch main && git pull
git log --oneline -5        # find the bad commit
git revert 9d41a2c          # new commit that undoes it
git push
code.caption: Reverting a merge commit needs -m 1. A squash merge avoids that: it is a normal commit.

scene.caption: The revert is one more commit on main. The broken change is undone, and still in history.

steps.title: Secrets in history stay in history
body: Revert has a blind spot. If a commit contained .env.local with Notely's Claude API key, reverting removes the file from the latest version only. The key is still readable in the old commit, forever.
Treat a committed secret as leaked. Create a new key, delete the old one, then add the file to .gitignore.

callout.text: Never rewrite shared history with a force push to hide it. Copies already exist on GitHub and on other laptops, and bots scan public repos for keys within minutes. Rotating the key is the real fix.

scene.caption: The revert removed the file from main, but the old commit still holds the key.

steps.title: Recap: save, branch, review, revert
body: Commits are named save points. Branches keep new work away from main, and main is what production runs. A pull request adds a preview, checks and a review before merging.
When something breaks, git revert undoes it with a new commit. A leaked secret is the exception: rotate it.

quiz.question: A merged pull request broke production ten minutes ago. Your teammate has already pulled main. What is the safest way to undo it?

options.text: git reset --hard to the old commit, then force push main.
options.why: That rewrites shared history. Your teammate's copy no longer matches GitHub, and their next push can bring the bad commit back or lose work.

options.text: Edit the broken files by hand until the error goes away.
options.why: Patching under pressure often adds new bugs, and the app stays broken while you work.

options.text: Revert the PR, which adds a new commit that undoes it.
options.why: A revert is a normal commit on top of main. Production returns to the old behavior, history stays intact, and you can fix the bug calmly on a branch.

quiz.question: Claude Code opened a PR called "Add tags". The diff also changes supabase/migrations, package-lock.json and middleware.ts. What do you do?

options.text: Ask why each unexpected file changed before merging.
options.why: A migration changes the live database and middleware runs on every request. Each one needs a reason that fits the feature. The lockfile change may be fine if a package was added on purpose.

options.text: Merge it. The checks are green, so it must be fine.
options.why: Checks only catch what they test. They cannot tell whether a change belongs in this PR at all.

options.text: Close the PR and write the feature yourself.
options.why: Unexpected files are a question, not proof of a bad PR. Asking is faster and you learn what changed.

quiz.question: Maya notices she committed .env.local with a live API key and pushed it. She reverts the commit. Is she safe?

options.text: Yes. The revert removed the file.
options.why: It removed the file from the newest version only. The old commit still contains the key, and anyone with the repo can read it.

options.text: No. She must create a new key, delete the old one, and ignore the file.
options.why: Once a secret is pushed, assume it is leaked. Rotating the key makes the leaked copy worthless, and .gitignore stops it happening again.

options.text: Yes, as long as the repo is private.
options.why: Private repos still get cloned, shared with tools and opened to collaborators. Private lowers the risk; it does not undo the leak.

takeaways: A commit is a named snapshot. Small commits with clear messages make bugs quick to find.
Do new work on a branch. main is what production runs.
A pull request gives you a preview URL, automatic checks and a diff to review before merging.
Undo a bad change with git revert, never with a force push on shared branches.
A secret that was ever committed is leaked. Rotate it, then add the file to .gitignore.
